# Computational Engine Principles {.unnumbered}

Part I opens the Stochastic Computer at its processor, the foundation model, and studies the single model call from which the H·S·A exposures are measured. One call runs one step, carries nothing beyond its prompt, and holds zero ambient authority, so it adds none of the three exposures. What it produces is a proposal, and a proposal changes nothing until the runtime admits it (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}). Part I therefore asks what a proposal costs and when buying more proposals makes the system more likely to succeed. The first answer comes from the hardware that generates each token.

::: {#pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding .callout-principle title="Memory-bandwidth-bounded decoding"}

**Invariant**: At small batch sizes each decode step reads the full weight tensor from high-bandwidth memory to emit one token per stream, so per-token latency is set by weight bytes divided by memory bandwidth, not by compute. An output token therefore costs about two orders of magnitude more wall-clock time than a prompt token processed during prefill. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-processor-cost.

**Implication**: Batching restores arithmetic intensity for a serving fleet, but an agent's own trajectory runs at batch size one because each step waits on the previous observation. The runtime controls latency by shortening outputs through interface design, by canceling doomed generations early, and by keeping per-token control work such as grammar masking on the accelerator.

:::

Decode cost prices a single proposal. Deliberation buys more of them, through longer reasoning, more candidates, or feedback from tools, and the question becomes when that extra spend pays.

::: {#pri-vol3-test-time-scaling .callout-principle title="Evidence-bounded deliberation"}

**Invariant**: Extra inference compute raises verified task success only when it acquires evidence that separates valid candidates from invalid ones. Longer generation and unguided resampling reuse the same parameters and the same prompt, so without a discriminating check they add cost faster than they add evidence. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-deliberation-insufficient-response.

**Implication**: The runtime should favor allocations that consult an external oracle, meter generation, verification, and tool cost in one ledger with hard ceilings, stop when marginal gain falls below marginal cost, and judge every deliberation policy against a single-candidate baseline at a matched budget.

:::

Whether a candidate counts as evidence depends on the check that judges it, and checks differ sharply in what they cost and what they can establish.

::: {#pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry .callout-principle title="The verification asymmetry"}

**Invariant**: Generating candidates is cheap, and so is running a stated mechanical check on one, such as a compiler pass, a schema, or a sealed test suite. Sound verification is not cheap. A check establishes only what it covers, deciding that it covers what the task requires is undecidable in general, and that decision cannot be delegated to the model whose output is being checked. When valid candidates are rare, a check that seldom errs still approves more invalid candidates than valid ones, and searching harder against an imperfect check selects for what it fails to test. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-deliberation-verification.

**Implication**: Search scales only as far as sound checks bound it. Learned verifiers may rank candidates to steer search, but the commit gate must be a deterministic check whose coverage matches the task's completion criteria, written and held where the agent cannot modify it. A task whose completion criteria have no mechanical form cannot be accepted autonomously, and a second model acting as judge does not supply one.

:::

Together, these principles price the processor's output and bound what search can make of it. @Sec-vol3-processor treats the model call as a contract whose cost is set by memory bandwidth, and @sec-vol3-deliberation spends inference compute on evidence and stops when evidence stops arriving. Every later part surrounds this processor with machinery, beginning with the state a trajectory must carry once it runs for more than one step.
